entry: Asterism of three bright stars in the constellation [[Orion (constellation)|Orion]]. Alnitak, Alnilam and Mintaka appear nearly equally spaced in a line from Earth, but each is a star system: Alnilam is a single star, Alnitak is triple and Mintaka quintuple. Their intense blue-white light comes from blue supergiants, and the systems together have a combined luminosity about a million times that of the Sun. Known under many names, including the Three Kings, the asterism has played a central role in navigation in the Northern Hemisphere since prehistoric times.

Archipelago and council area off the northern coast of [[Scotland]]. Part of the Northern Isles with [[Shetland]], it has about 70 islands, of which about 20 are inhabited. The largest, the Mainland, covers 523 sq km, and Kirkwall is the administrative center. Norway annexed the islands in 875, and in 1472 Scotland absorbed the earldom. Orkney has some of Europe's oldest and best-preserved [[Neolithic]] sites, including the Heart of Neolithic Orkney, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Agriculture is the main economic sector, and renewable energy generates more electricity than the islands need.

City, seat of Orange County, in central [[Florida]] (pop., 2020: 307,573). It is the state's fourth-most populous city and its most populous inland city. Tourism and conventions drive the economy. The [[Walt Disney World]] resort, opened in 1971, is one of the two largest tourist attractions in the area, and the Orange County Convention Center is the second-largest convention facility in the United States. Orlando International Airport is the 7th-busiest in the country.

Extinct [[Clade|clade]] of mainly herbivorous [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]] with a pelvic structure superficially similar to that of [[Bird|birds]]. The name, meaning bird-hipped, is misleading, since birds are theropod dinosaurs and only distantly related to the group. Members include the ceratopsians, such as [[Triceratops]]; the armored thyreophorans, such as stegosaurs and ankylosaurs; the pachycephalosaurs; and the ornithopods. Early forms were small, bipedal and fast runners, and some groups lived in herds. Many were partly covered in filamentous pelts, and debate continues over whether these were primitive feathers. The clade ranged from the Late [[Triassic]] until the [[Cretaceous]]-Paleogene extinction about 66 million years ago, contributing significantly to Mesozoic biodiversity.

Afroasiatic language of the Cushitic branch, spoken mainly in [[Ethiopia]], where about 85 percent of its speakers live. It is the most widely spoken Cushitic language and one of the five African languages with the largest mother-tongue populations. Smaller numbers speak it in northern [[Kenya]] and in other African countries. Oromo is one of Ethiopia's official working languages and the working language of several regions. It is a language of primary education in Oromia, Harari, Dire Dawa, Benishangul-Gumuz and Addis Ababa.It is officially written in the [[Latin script|Latin script]], although traditional scripts are also used informally. Under Haile Selassie's government, Oromo was de facto banned in education, conversation and administration.

Child whose parents have died, are unknown or have permanently abandoned them. In common usage, only a child who has lost both parents through death is called an orphan. [[UNICEF]] and UNAIDS, however, count any child who has lost one parent as an orphan: a maternal orphan has lost a mother, a paternal orphan a father, and a double orphan both. Wars, epidemics and poverty have produced many orphans. After the Second World War, estimates for Europe ranged from 1,000,000 to 13,000,000. Orphans are relatively rare in developed countries but numerous in war-torn nations such as [[Afghanistan]]. In the United States, about 2 million children, or 2.7 percent, have a deceased mother or father.

Residential institution, or group home, devoted to the care of [[Orphan|orphans]] and other children who cannot be raised by their families. Government-run orphanages were phased out in most developed countries in the latter half of the 20th century, as it became generally accepted that they harm children's emotional wellbeing. Government support now goes instead to the family unit. Some large international charities still fund orphanages, but most are founded by smaller charities and religious groups. In some developing countries, orphanages may recruit children to secure funding. Romanian orphanages, such as those in [[Bucharest]], were expanded after [[Nicolae Ceaușescu]] banned abortion and birth control to boost the population and workforce. Early charitable institutions included the Foundling Hospital, founded in London in 1741 by sea captain Thomas Coram.

Thracian bard, musician and prophet in [[Greek mythology]]. His music could charm animals, trees and even stones, and he traveled with Jason and the Argonauts. He attempted to retrieve his wife, Eurydice, from the underworld, and was later killed by the maenads of [[Dionysus]]. Orpheus was regarded as the founder of the Orphic mysteries, and works including the Orphic Hymns were attributed to him. Most ancient writers believed he was a real person, though [[Aristotle]] reportedly denied it.

American actor, director and filmmaker, remembered for innovative work in film, radio and theater. He co-founded the Mercury Theatre with John Houseman. His 1938 radio adaptation of [[H. G. Wells]]'s novel *The War of the Worlds* led some listeners to believe a Martian invasion was occurring, and it brought him Hollywood offers. His first film, *Citizen Kane* (1941), which he co-wrote, produced, directed and starred in, is consistently ranked among the greatest films ever made. He directed 12 other features, including *The Magnificent Ambersons* (1942), *Othello* (1951) and *Touch of Evil* (1958). Welles struggled for creative control within the [[Studio system|studio system]] and later often failed to secure financing as an independent filmmaker. A 2002 British Film Institute poll voted him the greatest film director ever.

Collective term for the traditionalist branches of contemporary [[Judaism]]. The movement regards the [[Torah]], both written and oral, as literally revealed by God on Mount Sinai and faithfully transmitted since. It advocates strict observance of Jewish law, or halakha, and observant members keep the Sabbath and kosher dietary laws, pray three times a day and study the Torah often. Doctrines include bodily resurrection and the future reign of a Messiah who will restore the Temple in [[Jerusalem]]. The movement is not a centralized denomination. Its Haredi branch is more conservative and reclusive, while Modern Orthodox Jews engage more with secular society. The earliest known use of the term dates from 1795. Orthodox Judaism is the largest Jewish religious group, with over 2 million practicing adherents.

Adherence to a purported correct or mainstream creed, especially in religion. The word derives from Greek for correct opinion. In Christianity, orthodoxy refers to doctrines defined by the early creeds and ecumenical councils. The homoousian doctrine, which defined Jesus as both God and man, prevailed over the teaching of [[Arius]] and became orthodoxy in most Christian contexts. After the 1054 Great Schism, both the Western [[Catholic Church]] and the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]] considered themselves orthodox and catholic. Oriental Orthodox Churches separated from Chalcedonian Christianity after the Council of Chalcedon in AD 451. [[Sunni Islam]] is sometimes called Orthodox Islam, and the [[Theravada]] school is considered the most orthodox form of Buddhism.

Set of conventions for writing a language, including norms of spelling, punctuation, word boundaries, capitalization, hyphenation and emphasis. Most established languages have standardized writing systems that show less dialect variation than speech. Standardization can fossilize pronunciation patterns no longer routinely heard, as in would and should. Differences can also be deliberate: [[Noah Webster]] introduced visible differences between American and British spelling, such as honor and honor. Some nations have language academies, such as the Académie Française in France and the Royal Spanish Academy in Spain, but English has no such authority. Newspapers of record and academic journals often enforce a style guide. The English word is first attested in the 15th century, from Ancient Greek words meaning correct and to write.

Order of [[Insect|insects]] comprising [[Grasshopper|grasshoppers]], [[Locust|locusts]], [[Cricket (insect)|crickets]] and katydids, with more than 20,000 species worldwide. The order divides into two suborders: Caelifera, which includes grasshoppers and locusts, and Ensifera, which includes crickets and katydids. Insects produce sound, called stridulation, by rubbing wings or legs together, and they hear through a tympanum in the front tibia or on the first abdominal segment. The forewings are narrow and hardened at the base, folding over fan-like hindwings. Life cycles are incomplete metamorphosis: nymphs resemble adults but lack wings until their final molt. The name comes from Greek for straight and wing. The order evolved about 300 million years ago, and locust swarms can devastate crops.

Asian cultivated rice, the more common of the two rice species grown as a cereal. The other is African rice, *O. glaberrima*. *Oryza sativa* was first domesticated in the [[Yangtze|Yangtze]] River basin in China. Its genome of 430 Mbp across 12 chromosomes makes it easy to genetically modify, and it is a [[Model organism|model organism]] for the study of cereals and monocots. Two major subspecies are recognized: the sticky, short-grained japonica and the nonsticky, long-grained indica. Japonica is grown mainly submerged in Japan and in temperate East Asia, while indica is grown mostly in lowlands throughout tropical Asia. Grain colors include white, brown, black and red.

Designated city in the Kansai region of [[Honshu]], Japan, and capital of Osaka Prefecture (pop., 2025: 2.8 million). It is Japan's third-most populous city proper, after the special wards of [[Tokyo]] and [[Yokohama]], and the largest part of the Keihanshin metropolitan area, which has more than 19 million inhabitants. Osaka was traditionally Japan's economic hub. It briefly served as the imperial capital in the seventh and eighth centuries, and it flourished during the [[Edo period]] as a center of Japanese culture. After the [[Meiji Restoration]], it became the industrial hub of the Meiji and Taishō eras. It is now a major financial center, home to the Osaka Exchange and the headquarters of [[Panasonic]] and Sharp.

Saudi-born militant, founder and first leader of [[Al-Qaeda|al-Qaeda]]. In 1984 he co-founded Maktab al-Khidamat to recruit foreigners for the Afghan mujahideen resisting Soviet occupation, and in 1988 he founded al-Qaeda. Expelled from Saudi Arabia in 1991, he moved to Sudan and then returned to Afghanistan, which the [[Taliban|Taliban]] came to control. Al-Qaeda bombed U.S. embassies in East Africa in 1998. Its attacks of September 11, 2001, killed 2,977 victims and led to the U.S.-led [[War on terror|war on terror]]. He lived in a compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, until U.S. Navy SEALs killed him in a raid codenamed Operation Neptune Spear. Polls show that Muslims at large have a negative view of him, while many Islamists consider him heroic.

Japanese [[Manga|manga]] artist, cartoonist and animator, often called the father of manga. His *New Treasure Island* (1947) began what became known as the manga revolution. He went on to create some of Japan's most influential series, including *Astro Boy*, *Princess Knight* and *Kimba the White Lion* for children and *Black Jack* and *Phoenix* for adults. Inspired by Walt Disney films and the Chinese animated film *Princess Iron Fan*, he also worked extensively in animation and founded Mushi Productions. He produced over 700 manga series. Often considered the Japanese equivalent of [[Walt Disney]], he is commemorated by a museum in Takarazuka dedicated to his life and work.

Brazilian architect and a key figure in [[Modern architecture|modern architecture]]. He is best known for the civic buildings he designed for [[Brasília]], a planned city that became Brazil's capital in 1960, including the National Congress, the Cathedral of Brasília and the Palácio do Planalto. He collaborated with [[Le Corbusier]] and others on the United Nations headquarters in New York. His exploration of reinforced concrete and his abstract forms and curves were highly influential. His other works include the Edifício Copan in [[São Paulo]] and the Niterói Contemporary Art Museum. Over a career of 78 years he designed approximately 600 projects. Because of his left-wing politics and involvement with the Brazilian Communist Party, he left Brazil after the 1964 military coup, opened an office in Paris and returned in 1985. He won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1988.

South African former [[Paralympic Games|Paralympic]] sprinter, double amputee and convicted murderer. Born without fibulas, he had both legs amputated below the knee in infancy. In 2011 he became the first amputee to win a nondisabled world track medal. In 2013 he shot and killed his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp, in his [[Pretoria]] home, claiming he had mistaken her for an intruder. The Supreme Court of Appeal convicted him of murder in 2015. He was released on parole in 2024 after serving 8.5 years in prison.

Irish author, poet and playwright and a key figure in the Aestheticism movement. His comedies, including *An Ideal Husband* and *The Importance of Being Earnest* (both 1895), made him one of the most successful playwrights of late-Victorian London. His Gothic novel, *The Picture of Dorian Gray* (1890), explored hedonism and moral decay, and his wit and flamboyant dress made him one of the best-known personalities of his day. In 1895 he was convicted of gross indecency with other men and sentenced to two years' hard labor, which broke his health and finances. In prison he wrote *De Profundis*, a long letter about his spiritual journey. After his release he moved to France and Italy, where he wrote *The Ballad of Reading Gaol* (1898), a poem about prison life.

Repetitive or periodic variation, typically in time, of some measure about a central value or between two or more states. Familiar examples include a swinging [[Pendulum|pendulum]] and [[Alternating current|alternating current]]. Oscillations occur throughout science: the beating of the human heart, business cycles in economics, predator-prey population cycles in ecology, geothermal geysers and the vibration of guitar strings. In a simple mechanical system, a weight on a spring is pulled back toward equilibrium by a restoring force proportional to its displacement, as described by [[Hooke's law|Hooke's law]]. This produces [[Simple harmonic motion|simple harmonic motion]]. The term vibration is used for mechanical oscillation. In process control, unwanted rapid oscillation is called chattering or flapping.

Electronic test instrument that graphically displays the varying [[Voltage|voltages]] of one or more signals as a function of time. Its main purpose is capturing information on electrical signals for debugging, analysis or characterization. Displayed waveforms reveal properties such as [[Amplitude|amplitude]] and [[Frequency|frequency]], rise time and distortion, and modern digital instruments calculate these directly. Oscilloscopes are used in science, engineering, biomedicine, automotive work and telecommunications. Early high-speed measurements used an electro-mechanical oscillograph invented by André Blondel in 1893, which was superseded by instruments using a cathode-ray tube. Probes usually have a resistor ten times the instrument's input impedance, giving a 0.1 (−10×) attenuation factor that helps isolate the probe cable's capacitive load from the signal.

Indian guru and founder of the Rajneesh movement, a [[New religious movement|new religious movement]]. He rejected institutional religion and taught a form of [[Meditation|meditation]] called dynamic meditation. In 1981 the movement shifted to the United States, where he established the commune Rajneeshpuram in [[Oregon]]. Legal battles curtailed its success, and in 1985 he was deported on immigration-related charges, after which 21 countries denied him entry. He returned to [[Pune]], where his ashram is now the Osho International Meditation Resort.

Ancient Egyptian god of fertility, agriculture, the afterlife, the dead and resurrection. He is classically depicted with a pharaoh's beard, mummy-wrapped legs and a crook and flail. In myth, his brother [[Set (deity)|Set]] killed and dismembered him, and his sister-wife [[Isis]] gathered the pieces and wrapped his body so that he could return to life. He then became lord of the dead and the underworld, and pharaohs came to be associated with him in death. His cult linked him to the annual flooding of the [[Nile]] and the renewal of vegetation. Worship is first attested from the middle of the Fifth Dynasty (25th century BCE), though he was likely worshipped earlier. Most knowledge of the myth comes from the Pyramid Texts and from Greek writers such as [[Plutarch]].

German military officer and war criminal who commanded a penal unit of the Waffen-SS, the Dirlewanger Brigade. Composed largely of convicts and other prisoners, the unit is considered among the most notorious Waffen-SS formations. He served mainly in Poland and Belarus, where he may have been responsible for around 120,000 killed in Belarus and up to 30,000 killed in [[Warsaw]], most of them non-combatants. His unit took part in the suppression of the Warsaw Uprising. He deserted in 1945, was captured by French authorities and died in Allied custody.
